content.overview: Technician I workers must recognize common cultivation hazards, apply routine controls within their authority, and stop or escalate work when a condition cannot be controlled safely.

vocabulary.definition: A source or condition with the potential to cause injury, illness, damage, or loss.
The combination of likelihood and severity of harm from a hazard.
A deliberate pause in work when conditions are unsafe, prohibited, or outside the worker's authority.

sections.title: Recognize the real work environment
sections.body: NIOSH identifies chemical, biological, ergonomic, physical, electrical, fire, cut, slip, trip, fall, heat, noise and ultraviolet-light hazards in cannabis work. A technician should notice obvious hazards instead of normalizing them because they are common.

sections.title: Control or escalate
sections.body: The preferred response is to remove or reduce a hazard through the strongest authorized control. Workers should not bypass safeguards or improvise repairs. If the assigned procedure cannot control the hazard, the correct response is to stop or isolate the task where authorized and escalate.

workedExamples: A hose crossing a main aisle is rerouted or secured under procedure rather than left as a repeated trip hazard.
Visible electrical damage near a wet area is taken out of use and escalated rather than investigated live by an unqualified worker.
commonMistakes: Treating a familiar hazard as acceptable because no injury has occurred yet.
Attempting a repair outside training or authorization.
content.practicalApplication: Inspect a mock cultivation room, identify hazards, and classify each response as routine control, stop/isolate, or escalation.
content.summary: Safe cultivation work requires hazard recognition, proportionate control, and clear authority boundaries. Correct escalation is part of competent performance.

blocks.title: Start with observation, not normalization
blocks.body: A wet aisle, damaged cord, unstable ladder, blocked walkway, sharp tool, leaking line, unguarded moving part, chemical splash risk, hot work area, or unsafe gas condition should not become invisible simply because workers see it every day. Recognition comes before production pressure.

blocks.alt: Simplified cultivation room showing irrigation water approaching damaged electrical equipment, a blocked aisle, an unstable ladder, an exposed cutting tool, high-intensity lighting, and a carbon-dioxide life-safety alarm, with a reminder to scan for other task-specific exposures.
blocks.caption: Use a deliberate room scan: people, pathways, equipment, environment, materials, and alarms.

blocks.title: Four questions for a pre-task hazard scan

items.title: People
items.body: What can injure or expose a worker during this task?

items.title: Crop and contamination
items.body: What could spread contamination or damage crop material?

items.title: Equipment and environment
items.body: What equipment, alarm, pathway, or environmental condition is outside its normal controlled state?

items.title: Authority
items.body: Is the required response inside your training, assigned procedure, and authorization?

blocks.title: Recognition is not repair authority
blocks.body: Recognizing a damaged electrical device, unsafe alarm condition, failed guard, or other technical fault does not automatically authorize a Technician I worker to open, repair, bypass, or troubleshoot it. Stop or isolate where the site procedure authorizes that action, then escalate.

blocks.alt: Flowchart showing a technician observing a hazard, checking for an authorized routine control, applying and verifying that control when permitted, or stopping, isolating where authorized, and escalating when the task cannot proceed safely. Life-safety alarms direct the worker to the posted emergency procedure.
blocks.caption: A practical decision model for routine controls, stop-work, isolation within authorization, escalation, and emergency response.

blocks.title: Routine control versus unauthorized technical repair

left.label: Routine control
left.body: A hose partly blocks an aisle and the approved hanger is available. Place the hose on the hanger, verify the path is clear, and continue according to procedure.

right.label: Technical fault
right.body: A powered device has visible cord damage near water. Do not open or test the wiring. Stop use, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate to the qualified person or team.

blocks.title: Water approaching damaged electrical equipment
blocks.setting: You enter a corridor and see irrigation water spreading toward a powered device with visible cord damage. The task list says irrigation must begin immediately.
blocks.prompt: What should control the next action?
options: Continue because the task is scheduled
Dry only the visible water and keep using the device
Stop the task, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate the electrical condition
Open the device to see whether the wire is actually energized
blocks.answer: Stop the task, prevent exposure where authorized, and escalate the electrical condition.
blocks.feedback: Production timing does not override an uncontrolled electrical hazard. Technician I should not perform unauthorized electrical investigation or repair.

blocks.title: Classify the first response
blocks.instructions: For each condition, classify the first response as routine control, stop/isolate, escalation, or emergency response. Then state what observation or rule supports your choice.
prompts: A hose partly blocks an aisle and can be placed on the approved hanger.
A ladder has a damaged step.
An unknown life-safety alarm is sounding in an enriched room.
A small spill is fully covered by the site's routine spill procedure.
A powered hand tool has a damaged cord.
A cart blocks a marked emergency route.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Safe routine cultivation work depends on noticing hazards early, using the strongest authorized control available, and treating stop-work and escalation as competent performance—not as failure to finish the task.
